distinguishing_features: Uses Rayleigh (surface) acoustic emission wave propagation analysis for subsurface shear micro-crack nucleation instead of vibration phase/envelope demodulation.
Detects crack initiation directly via high-frequency (10-100 kHz) stress-wave emission rather than inferring stiffness modulation from mesh-phase shift.
Derives sensor spacing from Rayleigh wavelength at the emission frequency (5·λ_R) rather than using existing speed-corrected reference signals.
parsed.objective_technical_problem: Detect subsurface shear micro-crack nucleation that precedes visible shelling damage in rail steel early enough to warn before failure, using surface-propagating elastic waves rather than macro-scale vibration signatures.
parsed.viable_reason: The design-point claim (0.1 mm crack sensitivity from λ/500 scattering) and the 5 dB/event-rate thresholds are physically implausible and unsupported; AE micro-crack emission in operating rail is swamped by rolling-contact noise and the detection sensitivity is vastly overstated.
parsed.non_obvious_reason: Applying surface Rayleigh-wave acoustic emission to detect subsurface micro-crack nucleation is a genuine mechanism departure from the phase-demodulation approach of the closest art, not a routine parameter change.
